A sense of place

A closer look at the places, textures and moments that make a journey.

The idea

Most trips are planned around the high sun. Ours are planned around its absence.

Every picture we are proud of was made in the minutes either side of sunrise and sunset, when the light is soft, the sky is blue and a place finally looks like itself. So we plan each expedition around those minutes, and fill the rest of the day with scouting, sleep and very good food.

8guests per trip, never more
2guides: a photographer and a local
20minutes of blue light on a good evening

How a trip unfolds

Five stops, one long evening.

1

The brief

A call a month before: what you shoot, what you want to shoot, what you are afraid of. We build the week around you.

2

Arrival

We land, drop bags and walk to the first location while there is still light, no itinerary, just orientation.

3

Scout by day

Mornings are for walking the ground we will use at dusk. Light changes everything, so we plan the angles in advance.

4

Blue hour

Out an hour before the light turns, home when it is gone. Eight photographers, two guides, tripods in a line.

5

Review

Every evening we edit together over dinner: three keepers each, one honest note, then sleep. Prints follow within a month.

Good to know

Questions before you book.

Do I need a professional camera?

No. Any camera with manual mode and a tripod is enough. We have mirrorless loaners for a small deposit.

How fit do I need to be?

Each trip lists a level. Most are walks under five kilometres on uneven ground, with some dark early starts.

What if the weather ruins the night?

Weather is part of the picture. We keep two spare evenings in every itinerary and move locations to chase clear sky.

Can I come on my own?

Most guests do. Rooms are single by default and the group is small enough to feel like friends by day three.

Not sure which one?

Ask us, we love this question.

Tell us what you like to photograph and how you like to travel. We will point you to the right trip, even if it is not ours.

The itinerary

Nine days, in order.

1

Day 1–2 · Arrive in Svolvær

Land, drop bags and walk to the harbour for a first look at the light. Briefing over dinner.

2

Day 3 · Reine at dusk

Red cabins, black water and the first aurora forecast. Our first real blue hour.

3

Day 4–5 · The beaches

Haukland and Uttakleiv at low tide, then a long evening on the dunes with the sea at our back.

4

Day 6 · Weather day

Rest, edit and print. If the sky opens, we go; if not, nobody is sorry.

5

Day 7–8 · Henningsvær

Football pitch on a rock, harbour reflections and the last aurora window of the trip.

6

Day 9 · Farewell

A last sunrise at the fjord, a final edit over breakfast and a flight home with a full card.

Included

  • 8 nights in fishing cabins (shared kitchens, private rooms)
  • All breakfasts, five dinners, a harbour-side seafood night
  • Minibus and boat transfers
  • Three signed A3 prints

Bring

  • Camera with manual mode, wide lens, sturdy tripod
  • Warm layers and spikes for your boots
  • Flights to Svolvær (we advise on timing)
Good to know
What are the odds of seeing aurora?

In a nine-day window, high. We have seen it on 8 of the last 9 trips, but we never promise a sky.

How cold does it get?

Around −5 to −10 °C at night, with wind. We send a layering guide and lend spikes.

Is it suitable for beginners?

Yes. We run a short exposure workshop on day one.

What is the cancellation policy?

Full refund up to 90 days before departure, 50% up to 45 days. Insurance is required.

pages.story:
Field notesLofoten, Norway8 min readBy Mara Lindqvist

ElevenMinutes

of blue, on a flat sea, with the lighthouse still lit. A long evening told in the order it happened.

Moon, sea and the Hamnøy light, 21:40. 25 s at f/4, ISO 800.

At 21:12 the sun had been gone for an hour and the sea had gone the colour of a bruise. Nobody spoke. Eight tripods stood in a loose line on the rocks, and the only sound was the shutter of someone who could not wait.

The trick with blue hour is that it is not an hour. On this coast, in January, it is closer to eleven minutes: the sky has to be dark enough that the lighthouse beam reads, and bright enough that the water still holds a colour. Miss either end and you have a nice picture of nothing.

What we got wrong, twice

The first night we arrived late and shot into the sun. The second we arrived early and shot the wrong rock. On the third we sat on the beach for forty minutes with our backs to the view, and turned around together at 21:29.

Patience is a lens, and it is the only one you cannot lose.

Here is what I tell every group on the walk down: pick one foreground, one frame and one setting. When the colour arrives, do not change any of them. Change your breathing instead.

Same evening, 23:05, looking the other way. 10 s at f/2.8, ISO 3200.

The settings, for the record

FrameExposureISOLens
Lighthouse25 s · f/480024 mm
Reflection8 s · f/5.640035 mm
Aurora10 s · f/2.8320020 mm

None of it is secret. All of it is boring. The magic is being on the rocks at 21:29 with your hands warm and your mind quiet.
